<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, the project type is a self-hosted, full-stack bookmark manager built with Django as the backend and a Node.js-driven frontend for JavaScript component compilation (with Svelte and regular JavaScript components). Here’s how to approach drawing an accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Identify Main Components:
   • Backend (Django): Represent the “bookmarks” directory as the core application. This component includes models, views, API endpoints (in bookmarks/api), management commands, signals, middlewares, migrations, and the admin panel. It also contains the REST API, authentication routines (including SSO via OIDC/proxies), and the business logic for handling bookmarks, tags, and archiving.
   • Frontend Assets: Depict the “bookmarks/frontend” folder, which contains JavaScript files, Svelte components, utility scripts, CSS and styles. This frontend component is used in both serving the user interface (HTML templates from the backend) and handling dynamic interactions (e.g., tag auto-completion, modal dialogs, form behaviors).
   • Database: Although not explicitly detailed in the files, the migration files indicate a persistent database backend (commonly used with Django, likely PostgreSQL). Represent the database as a separate component that the Django backend interacts with.
   • DevOps & Deployment: Include components for deployment such as Docker (docker-compose.yml, Dockerfiles), configuration files (uwsgi.ini, supervisord.conf), and GitHub Actions (in .github/workflows) to illustrate continuous integration/deployment.
   • Documentation & Assets: Show a side component representing the “docs” directory (documentation built with Astro and Markdown) and assets (logos, design files). This supports developers and end users but is separate from the runtime architecture.
   • Testing & Scripts: Represent integration tests (pytest, tests and tests_e2e directories) and custom scripts (in scripts/) for building, releasing, and managing backups, which ensure quality and deployment automation.

2. Show Relationships and Data Flows:
   • Draw directional arrows from the Client (browser) to the Frontend and from the Frontend to the Django Backend, indicating how HTTP requests are sent to the backend for both UI rendering and REST API calls.
   • Show the backend’s interaction with the Database, especially for CRUD operations on bookmarks, tags, and user profiles.
   • Indicate the flow for asynchronous or background processes – for example, the management commands (backup, auto-tagging, asset caching) and service integrations (e.g., Internet Archive integration for archiving websites).
   • For the development lifecycle, depict the CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions and Docker containers that encapsulate the environment setup (DevContainers, Docker images).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Emphasize the Model-View-Controller (or model–template–view in Django) pattern used in the backend. Show separation between data (models), presentation (templates, static assets) and control (views, APIs).
   • Call out the integration of a REST API layer that supports external integrations and browser-based API consumption.
   • Note the clear separation between development tasks (Node.js for frontend asset building) and the runtime server (Django), which is a crucial design element.

4. Include Relevant Technologies:
   • Backend: Python 3.12, Django (with its built-in ORM, middleware, and templating system). Also note Django-specific aspects such as migrations, signals, and management commands.
   • Frontend: Node.js, npm, Svelte components, and JavaScript utilities for handling dynamic UI behaviors.
   • Database: Likely PostgreSQL (inferred from standard Django usage and Docker configurations).
   • Docker & DevOps: Docker Compose, Dockerfiles, GitHub workflows, and scripting for deployment and testing.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Since this is a full-stack application, segregate the diagram into distinct frontend and backend layers along with the database. Indicate the API endpoints that the frontend calls.
   • Use boxes to represent each main component (Client, Frontend assets, Django Backend, Database, CI/CD pipeline/Containerization) and connect them with arrows to illustrate request-response cycles and internal workflows.
   • Use different colors or shapes for distinct types of components (for example, blue boxes for backend modules, green for frontend, orange for infrastructure components like databases, and gray for CI/CD and test components).

6. Specific Elements to Include in the Diagram:
   • Clear Labels: Each component should be clearly labeled (e.g., “Django Backend – Bookmarks Application”, “Frontend – JavaScript & Svelte Components”, “Database”, “CI/CD & Docker Infrastructure”).
   • Directional Arrows: Use arrows to show the data flow. For instance, show how user requests flow from the Browser to the Django server, and how API or static content requests flow from the frontend components.
   • Color Coding/Shapes: Distinguish between presentation layers (frontend), business logic (backend), data storage (database) and deployment/integration components (containerization, CI/CD). This visual distinction can be achieved by using different colors and shapes for each type.
   • Additional Details: Optionally annotate the diagram with key technologies (e.g., “Python/Django”, “Node.js/Svelte”, “PostgreSQL”), and point out specific functionalities such as the REST API, authentication modules, and backup/auto-tagging services.

By following these instructions, you (the principal software engineer) can produce a detailed and accurate system design diagram that captures all essential components and interactions in the Linkding bookmark manager project. This clear separation of concerns and thorough mapping of data flow will help both current and future contributors better understand the application’s architecture.
</explanation>
